title: Accessibility Deep Dive — WCAG, ARIA, and Keyboard Patterns

subChunks.title: Accessibility Deep Dive — WCAG, ARIA, and Keyboard Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: WCAG 2.1 AA is the legal standard for web accessibility in most jurisdictions. Failing it is not just an ethical failure — it's a legal liability. React's component model makes it easy to build inaccessible UIs by default: click handlers on divs, custom controls that aren't keyboard navigable, dynamic content that doesn't announce itself to screen readers. This lesson covers the patterns that make React UIs genuinely accessible.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The WCAG principles — POUR

  • Perceivable: information must be presentable in ways users can perceive. Alt text for images, captions for video, sufficient colour contrast.
  • Operable: interface components must be operable by keyboard, no timing traps, no seizure-inducing content.
  • Understandable: information and UI operation must be understandable. Clear error messages, predictable navigation.
  • Robust: content must be robust enough to be interpreted by assistive technologies. Valid HTML, correct ARIA usage.

ARIA — when and how to use it

// Rule 1: Don't use ARIA if native HTML semantics cover it
// ❌ Redundant — button already has role="button":
<button role="button">Click</button>

// ✅ ARIA needed — custom element, no native role:
<div
  role="button"
  tabIndex={0}
  onKeyDown={e => e.key === 'Enter' && handleClick()}
  onClick={handleClick}
>
  Custom button
</div>

// Labelling — aria-label vs aria-labelledby:
<button aria-label="Close modal">✕</button>

<h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm Quest Acceptance</h2>
<div role="dialog" aria-labelledby="dialog-title">...</div>

// Live regions — announce dynamic content:
<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
  {statusMessage} {/* Screen readers announce changes */}
</div>

// role="status" is shorthand for aria-live="polite":
<p role="status">{toastMessage}</p>

Keyboard navigation patterns

// Tab order — use tabIndex correctly:
// tabIndex={0} — adds to natural tab order
// tabIndex={-1} — focusable via JS, not in tab order
// Avoid positive tabIndex values

// Focus trapping in modals:
function useFocusTrap(containerRef, isActive) {
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isActive) return;
    const el = containerRef.current;
    const focusable = el.querySelectorAll(
      'button, [href], input, select, textarea, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])'
    );
    const first = focusable[0];
    const last = focusable[focusable.length - 1];

    function trap(e) {
      if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
      if (e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) {
        e.preventDefault();
        last.focus();
      } else if (!e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) {
        e.preventDefault();
        first.focus();
      }
    }

    el.addEventListener('keydown', trap);
    first.focus();
    return () => el.removeEventListener('keydown', trap);
  }, [isActive]);
}

Skip links

// Allow keyboard users to skip to main content:
<a href="#main-content" className="skip-link">
  Skip to main content
</a>

<main id="main-content">...</main>

// CSS — visible only on focus:
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  transform: translateY(-100%);
  &:focus { transform: translateY(0); }
}

Testing accessibility

// jest-axe — automated a11y testing:
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from 'jest-axe';
expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

test('has no accessibility violations', async () => {
  const { container } = render(<QuestCard quest={mockQuest} />);
  const results = await axe(container);
  expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
});

Vex: "Automated tools catch about 30% of accessibility issues — they're a floor, not a ceiling. The rest requires: keyboard-only navigation testing (unplug your mouse), screen reader testing (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on Mac), and users with disabilities in your test group. Automate what you can; test the rest manually."

storyBeats.text: A blind user opens the quest board with a screen reader. Nothing is announced. The custom dropdown isn't focusable. The 'Accept Quest' div doesn't respond to Enter. Vex opens the accessibility audit.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: WCAG is not a checkbox. It's a standard for ensuring every user can access your application. Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. The most common React failures: click handlers on divs, no focus management in modals, dynamic content that doesn't announce to screen readers, insufficient colour contrast.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Use native elements when possible — a button is keyboard accessible, screen reader announced, and correct by default. When you must build a custom control, use ARIA to communicate its role, state, and properties. Add keyboard handlers. Trap focus in modals. Test with a keyboard. Then test with a screen reader.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Make a set of inaccessible components accessible:

  • A div with onClick that acts as a button — replace with a button element or add ARIA + keyboard support
  • A form input with no label — add <label htmlFor> or aria-label
  • An error message that appears dynamically — add role="alert" so screen readers announce it
  • A modal that doesn't trap focus — implement a focus trap using useEffect

guidedPracticeTests.label: Toggle is keyboard accessible (button element or role=button)

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build an accessible <MenuButton> component implementing the WAI-ARIA Menu Button pattern. It should: toggle a menu with role="menu", trap focus within the open menu, support keyboard navigation (Arrow Up/Down moves through items, Enter/Space selects, Escape closes and returns focus to trigger), and announce the open/closed state via aria-expanded. Include jest-axe tests that verify no violations.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the WCAG POUR principles. Then walk through the three most common React accessibility failures and their fixes. Finally, explain why automated tools only catch 30% of accessibility issues — what do you need to test manually, and how?

options: Tells screen readers to announce the content of the element when it changes, after the user finishes their current action
Prevents the element from receiving keyboard focus
Marks the element as decorative (ignored by screen readers)
Indicates the element is politely styled
questions.answer: Tells screen readers to announce the content of the change, after the user finishes their current action
questions.explanation: aria-live='polite' creates a live region. When the content of the element changes, screen readers queue the announcement and read it after the current speech completes. Use it for non-urgent status updates (search results count, form success). aria-live='assertive' interrupts immediately — use only for urgent errors.

questions.prompt: Why must a modal trap focus?
options: Without focus trapping, keyboard users can Tab to elements behind the modal and interact with content that's visually hidden — breaking the user's mental model
Focus trapping is required by the HTML spec for dialog elements
Without trapping, the modal will close when focus leaves it
Focus trapping prevents screen readers from reading modal content
questions.answer: Without focus trapping, keyboard users can Tab to elements behind the modal and interact with content that's visually hidden — breaking the user's mental model
questions.explanation: When a modal is open, the background content is visually overlaid and inert. But keyboard users can still Tab to elements behind it if focus isn't trapped. They'd be interacting with invisible content — tabbing into a background form, activating background buttons. Focus trapping keeps the keyboard user's context inside the modal until they explicitly close it.

questions.prompt: A custom toggle switch uses a `div` with onClick. What is needed to make it fully accessible?
options: role='switch', aria-checked={isOn}, tabIndex={0}, and onKeyDown handling for Space/Enter to activate
Just adding tabIndex={0} makes it keyboard accessible
Wrapping it in a <form> makes it accessible
questions.answer: role='switch', aria-checked={isOn}, tabIndex={0}, and onKeyDown handling for Space/Enter to activate
questions.explanation: role='switch' tells screen readers it's a toggle. aria-checked communicates the on/off state. tabIndex={0} adds it to the tab order so keyboard users can reach it. onKeyDown handling for Space/Enter lets keyboard users activate it. Without all four, the control either can't be reached, can't be activated, or doesn't communicate its purpose/state to screen readers.

questions.prompt: An automated axe audit reports zero violations. Can you ship the component as accessible?
options: No — automated tools catch ~30% of issues. Manual keyboard navigation testing and screen reader testing are still required.
Yes — axe is comprehensive and catches all WCAG 2.1 violations
Yes, if combined with Lighthouse which covers the remaining 70%
No, but only for components with custom ARIA attributes
questions.answer: No — automated tools catch ~30% of issues. Manual keyboard navigation testing and screen reader testing are still required.
questions.explanation: Automated tools (axe, Lighthouse) check static rules: missing alt text, invalid ARIA, duplicate IDs, insufficient contrast. They can't evaluate: logical focus order, whether the keyboard flow makes sense, whether screen reader announcements are meaningful, or whether the component is usable by someone with a disability. Manual testing — keyboard-only navigation and a screen reader — catches the other 70%.
